strengths: Addresses an important practical problem (catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning) with a pragmatic approach that requires no pre-training data and doesn't modify the loss function

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, benchmarks, and scenarios (instruction fine-tuning and continual learning) with thorough ablation studies on update fraction and filtering strategies
Consistent empirical demonstration of reduced forgetting on general capability benchmarks (MMLU, Commonsense, GSM8K) while maintaining competitive fine-tuning performance

Clear and intuitive presentation of the core idea with helpful visualizations (Figure 1) and a useful toy example (Section 4) illustrating why selective parameter updates lead to convergence at closer minima
Systematic comparison of momentum-based vs. gradient-based vs. random parameter selection strategies, validating the design choice through empirical results
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 proves convergence only for a simplified GD version (Algorithm 2), not the momentum-based method actually used. The O(T^{-1/2}) rate is standard and provides no special insight into why MoFO should work

Limited novelty: The approach is essentially greedy BCD applied to Adam with momentum-magnitude filtering. While practical, this feels incremental relative to well-established BCD methods and recent work on parameter-efficient fine-tuning

Theory-practice gap: Motivation discusses gradient magnitude as an influence indicator, but the method uses momentum. Why momentum filtering fundamentally outperforms gradient filtering lacks rigorous justification (only Table 5 provides empirical comparison)

Modest empirical improvements: Performance gains are often small (Table 2: MoFO 47.7 vs Full FT 49.4 on GSM8K; Table 3: MoFO 33.7 vs L1-reg 33.8 on HumanEval; Table 4: only 1.5% gain over Replay). No statistical significance testing or error bars reported

Dataset-dependent hyperparameter tuning: Different α% values required for different experiments (5%-15%) with no principled guidance for selection. Figure 3 shows steep degradation beyond 20%, limiting practical applicability
Computational overhead not addressed: Sorting momentum magnitudes at each iteration has non-trivial cost, but this is never discussed or compared against baselines
Weak baseline configurations: L2 regularization uses λ₂=1e-3, which is relatively weak. Stronger regularization settings are not tested, and comparison is limited to relatively old baselines
Loss landscape visualization limitations: 2D projections (Figure 2) can be misleading for high-dimensional landscapes. Method for generating projections not clearly specified

Missing analysis of mechanism: No investigation of which layers/parameters are most frequently updated, or under what conditions MoFO provides maximum benefit (e.g., when parameter momentum magnitudes are heterogeneous vs. homogeneous)

strengths: Addresses the important problem of catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning with a practical approach that requires neither pre-training data nor loss function modification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and settings (instruction fine-tuning and continual learning) with diverse benchmarks
Clear algorithmic design with intuitive loss landscape visualizations (Figure 2) demonstrating that MoFO converges closer to pre-trained models
Consistent results across tasks showing MoFO reduces forgetting without significantly harming fine-tuning performance
Interesting toy example (Section 4) providing intuition about how selective parameter updates can avoid attractors
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: Theorem 1 proves convergence only for a simplified GD variant (Algorithm 2), not the momentum-based Adam variant (Algorithm 1) actually used in experiments. Authors acknowledge this limitation but provide no theoretical justification for the momentum-based design.

Weak justification for momentum-based selection: The paper does not convincingly explain why momentum magnitude should be a better importance signal than gradients. Table 5 shows only modest improvement of momentum-based over gradient-based BCD (45.4 vs 40.2 on GSM8K) without principled explanation.

Unjustified core hypothesis: The claim that smaller parameter distance from pre-training reduces forgetting relies on assumed correlation without causal justification. The 2D toy example is highly contrived and doesn't generalize to high-dimensional LLM landscapes.

Inconsistent and potentially unfair baseline comparisons: L1/L2 regularization use fixed hyperparameters without tuning, while MoFO's α% is task-specifically tuned (15% for MetaMathQA, 10% for Code-Alpaca, 5% for TRACE), raising fairness concerns.

Modest empirical improvements: MoFO achieves only marginal gains over simpler baselines—e.g., 47.7 vs 47.5 on GSM8K compared to HFT, which is far simpler. No statistical significance testing or error bars. On Code-Alpaca, L1-reg (33.8) slightly outperforms MoFO (33.7).

Limited novelty: The method is essentially greedy BCD applied to Adam. The simpler Half Fine-tuning baseline (random BCD) achieves comparable performance, questioning the contribution of momentum-based selection.

Experimental concerns: Only 2 epochs of training in some experiments is very short; limited model scale (only 7B and 1.1B tested); missing ablations (e.g., how sensitive is performance to α% across diverse tasks?); no documentation of how α% was selected for each task.
Presentation issues: Non-standard redefinition of 'minimum,' 2D loss landscape projections may not be representative of high-dimensional behavior, unclear generalization from toy example to real LLMs

strengths: Addresses practical problem of catastrophic forgetting with method requiring no pre-training data access
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (MetaMathQA, Code-Alpaca, TRACE) and diverse metrics (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, commonsense tasks)
Simple, practical method easy to implement and integrate with existing Adam optimizer
Convincing empirical evidence that MoFO converges ~20% of Adam's distance to pre-trained model (Figure 2), translating to better capability preservation
Solid ablation studies examining update fraction sensitivity and selection strategy comparisons (Tables 3, 5)
Consistent improvements in preserving general capabilities across different task domains and model sizes
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis is incomplete: Theorem 1 only covers simplified GD version (Algorithm 2), not the actual momentum-based MoFO; authors acknowledge convergence proof for full algorithm is non-trivial
Key design choice lacks theoretical justification: why momentum-based selection is better than gradient-based selection is shown empirically (Table 5) but not explained theoretically
Causal link between distance-to-pretrained and forgetting mitigation is assumed rather than rigorously established; toy example (Section 4) is illustrative but artificial
Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is greedy block coordinate descent with momentum selection, similar to Half Fine-tuning with different selection criterion
Hyperparameter α% requires task-specific tuning with significant sensitivity (Figure 3): 15% for MetaMathQA, 10% for Code-Alpaca, 5% for TRACE; no principled guidance for new tasks
Empirical improvements are modest (1-3%) and lack statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars across experiments
All experiments limited to 1-7B parameter models; scalability to larger models (70B+) and multimodal architectures unexplored
Insufficient explanation of implementation details: how are B parameter partitions determined exactly? What is computational overhead of top-α% selection per iteration?

strengths: Well-motivated approach with compelling empirical evidence for distance-forgetting correlation (Figures 1-2)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models, datasets, and metrics with good ablation studies
Practical advantages: no pre-training data needed, minimal memory/time overhead (4-5%), drop-in Adam replacement
Non-trivial convergence analysis (Theorem 1) showing MoFO maintains O(log T/√√T) rate despite selective updates
Excellent presentation, reproducibility, and implementation guidance
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: applying classical BCD with momentum filtering is incremental; choice of momentum filtering over gradients lacks principled justification

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 doesn't explain why distance mitigates forgetting; Theorem 2 uses artificial separable loss landscape unrealistic for neural networks; full-batch analysis doesn't cover mini-batch SGD in practice
Critical hyperparameter α% lacks principled selection, requires proxy dataset grid search (Section E), optimal values vary by model (5%-15%), undermining drop-in replacement claims

Modest empirical improvements often without statistical validation: Table 1 shows MoFO (47.7) underperforms Default FT (49.4) on fine-tuning; Table 6 shows marginal gains over LoRA (40.9 vs 40.2); no error bars or multiple runs reported

Problematic baseline comparisons: LoRA deliberately trains less (unfair comparison with full-parameter updates); missing modern continual learning baselines; Tables 8 shows CoFiTune and soft-masking competitive or better on fine-tuning

Parameter partitioning appears arbitrary: default PyTorch grouping lacks theoretical justification; head-level partitioning (G.4) performs worse (44.3→43.8) but not investigated; raises robustness questions
Incomplete analysis of when MoFO helps and no clear guidance on problem characteristics for applicability

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence (Figures 1-2) that distance from pre-trained model correlates with forgetting
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, datasets, and benchmarks with detailed ablations in appendices
Practical design with minimal overhead: no pre-training data required, 4-5% training time increase only
Honest discussion of limitations and acknowledgment of future work directions
Convergence analysis (Theorem 1) ensuring method maintains Adam's convergence rate
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines classical BCD with straightforward momentum-based filtering on Adam; concurrent works (Panda et al. 2024, Li et al. 2024) explore similar directions
Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 shows convergence equals Adam (no improvement), Theorem 2/Example 1 analyze toy 2D problems with artificial loss structure not reflective of neural networks
Marginal empirical improvements: Table 1 shows MoFO (44.3 avg general capability) vs HFT (43.8), GSM8K 47.7 vs 47.5; no statistical significance testing or error bars
Circular reasoning: paper establishes distance→forgetting correlation, then proposes method that by design stays close; lacks deep explanation of why momentum filtering specifically helps
New hyperparameter α% introduces tuning complexity; grid search guidelines (Appendix E) contradict claims of simplicity; Appendix G.3's post-hoc stability explanation is not rigorous

Key design choices poorly justified: distance metric (average L2 norm over blocks) lacks sensitivity analysis; parameter partitioning uses PyTorch defaults without principled justification (G.4 shows similar results with head-level partitioning)
Missing critical ablations: unclear how much momentum filtering vs. selective BCD contributes; Appendix G.3's stability hypothesis unproven
Modest scope limitations: supervised fine-tuning only (no RLHF), models up to 7B, no deployment scenarios; improvements are incremental rather than transformative

Presentation issues: important content relegated to appendices (distance calculation D.4, stability analysis G.3); Pareto frontier comparison uses linear interpolation not exhaustive search; 39-page paper could be more concise

Inconsistent baseline comparisons: LoRA performs surprisingly poorly on forgetting contrary to recent literature; L1/L2 regularization comparisons somewhat unfair (modify objective); unclear relationship to concurrent BCD work

strengths: Well-motivated approach with strong empirical evidence for distance-forgetting correlation across multiple settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple LLMs (Llama-2-7B, Gemma-2B, TinyLlama), datasets (MetaMathQA, PMC-LLaMA, TRACE), and diverse metrics with detailed ablations and comparisons
Practical efficiency: no pre-training data required, no additional memory overhead, only 4-5% computational cost; simple implementation using PyTorch defaults

Solid technical execution with convergence proof (Theorem 1) showing MoFO maintains Adam's convergence rate despite selective updates, comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3-4), and analysis of update stability
Consistent improvements in preserving general capabilities while maintaining fine-tuning performance across multiple benchmarks and a Pareto frontier analysis showing favorable trade-offs
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (loss landscapes), detailed algorithms, guidelines for hyperparameter selection, and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: work primarily adapts existing BCD with Gauss-Southwell rule to Adam optimizer via momentum filtering—a relatively straightforward combination. Related ideas exist (HFT, soft-masking, selective module updates); concurrent BCD-based approaches mentioned.

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 provides ℓ∞-norm convergence (weaker than standard ℓ1 results) without explaining why momentum filtering helps forgetting. Theorem 2 only addresses 2D toy problem; generalization to real high-dimensional non-convex settings unclear.

Modest empirical improvements: general capability gains often small (0.5-0.8% differences vs. baselines). Fine-tuning performance sometimes degrades (Table 3: GSM8K 45.4 vs. 49.4 for Default FT). Continual learning improvements also incremental (Table 2).
Hyperparameter α% requires grid search on proxy data; no principled selection method. Guidelines suggest 5-20% range but optimal value is dataset/model dependent, limiting practical applicability.

Limited analysis of when/why MoFO succeeds or fails: no investigation of task properties determining effectiveness, no failure case analysis, or characterization of when momentum filtering outperforms gradient filtering beyond Appendix G.3 empirical observations.

Experimental concerns: only 10% sampling of datasets used (unclear if results generalize); missing statistical significance tests; L1/L2 regularization baselines require storing pre-training weights (unfair comparison); some recent forgetting-aware methods not compared.
Reproducibility: no code release mentioned; key details relegated to appendix (distance metric, partitioning scheme); would benefit from released implementation and full dataset experiments.

Paper length (39 pages) with critical experimental details in appendix reduces readability; distance-forgetting connection is correlational, not causal; limited discussion of interaction with other regularization techniques.
